title: Fourier Symmetrization for Geometric Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Letao Wang, Abdel Lisser, Sreejith Sreekumar, Zeno Toffano
abstract: Geometric quantum machine learning incorporates symmetry into quantum models, but how symmetry shapes their expressivity and guides effective model design remains insufficiently understood. We address this question through the Fourier representation of quantum Fourier models (QFMs). Symmetry organizes the frequency spectrum into orbits and sums the Fourier coefficients within each orbit into a symmetrized coefficient. When QFM trainable layers form independent exact 2-designs, the variance of each symmetrized coefficient equals the sum of the coefficient variances in its orbit. For single-layer QFMs with $\varepsilon$-approximate 2-design trainable layers, we bound the deviation from this identity. The resulting bound for individual Fourier coefficients can be exponentially tighter than an existing bound. The hyperoctahedral group provides an example of orbit growth that can mitigate vanishing expressivity of the symmetrized coefficients. Symmetrization of QFMs over an elementary abelian 2-group also yields pure multivariate Chebyshev polynomial basis functions. We introduce randomized encoding, which implements invariant models without ancilla qubits or the additional circuit depth for quantum twirling. We evaluate the models as quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) on two-dimensional screened Poisson and stationary viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Under hard boundary constraints, QPINNs using exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieve the lowest mean errors in the two benchmarks, respectively.
summary: This work develops a rigorous framework for incorporating symmetry into Quantum Fourier Models (QFMs) for machine learning. By analyzing the Fourier spectrum, the authors derive tight bounds showing how symmetry constrains model expressivity. They validate this approach by demonstrating that symmetry-aware QPINNs achieve superior accuracy when solving complex physical PDEs.
main_problem: The paper addresses how symmetry constrains and shapes the expressivity of Quantum Fourier Models (QFMs) used in Geometric Quantum Machine Learning (GQML). It seeks to provide rigorous theoretical bounds on the performance of symmetry-enforced models.
main_result: Randomized encoding, which avoids deep circuits, achieves the lowest mean errors when using QPINNs to solve 2D PDEs like the screened Poisson and Hamilton-Jacobi equations.
method: The authors use Fourier analysis to decompose symmetry-invariant QFMs, deriving tight theoretical bounds on coefficient variances by analyzing the deviation from ideal 2-design assumptions.
model_or_system: The model is a Quantum Fourier Model (QFM) used as a Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Network (QPINN) to solve continuous Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) in 2D space.
key_observables: Mean error in solving PDEs (Screened Poisson, Stationary Viscous Hamilton-Jacobi), and the variance of symmetrized Fourier coefficients.
important_parameters: The approximation parameter $\epsilon$, the size of the symmetry group, and the dimensionality of the PDEs (2D).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the QFM viewpoint, the assumption of 2-design properties for trainable layers, and the use of randomized encoding to implement symmetry invariance without deep circuits.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes reference figures illustrating Fourier orbit decomposition and the comparison of various QPINN performance metrics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the symmetry problem in QFMs, developing the Fourier orbit decomposition theory, deriving tight mathematical bounds on coefficient variances, and finally validating the approach by applying it to solve specific 2D PDEs using randomized encoding.
why_interesting: The explicit connection between group theory (symmetry), spectral analysis (Fourier decomposition), and physical modeling (PDEs) provides a powerful, structured inductive bias for quantum machine learning applied to physical systems.
